Lagos Business School · Executive Education · Turning Data into Business Growth

Getting data you can trust

Day 2 · Get it · Tuesday 13 October 2026

Prof. Bongo Adi · Lagos Business School

Today

Today the room stops taking numbers on trust.


Somewhere between eleven and lunch, at least one table will present a finding with complete confidence that turns out to be an artefact of a bad join.

That is not a risk of the design. It is the design, and it is much cheaper to happen here than in a board paper.

2.1 · SQL as the lingua franca

09:15 — 10:15 · Six verbs, read rather than written

You are not going to learn to write SQL

You are going to learn to read, predict and audit it.


The test at the end of the hour is not “can you write this query?”

It is “can you say what this query will do to the data before you run it, and be right?”

Facilitator · Say plainly that composing from a blank page is over, and that it was never the valuable part. The blank page was the barrier to entry; everything past it was always the job.

Six ideas. Five are safe.

The idea SQL One word
1 Pick rows WHERE filter
2 Pick columns SELECT choose
3 Make new columns SELECT ... AS derive
4 Collapse to groups GROUP BY summarise
5 Put in order ORDER BY arrange
6 Bring tables together JOIN combine

Five of the six fail loudly: you get an error, or an answer that is obviously wrong. The sixth fails quietly, which is why it gets its own session this afternoon.

Read it aloud, in execution order

SELECT p.category, COUNT(DISTINCT s.sku) AS skus,
       SUM(s.revenue_ngn) AS revenue, AVG(s.discount_pct) AS avg_discount
FROM 'fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
JOIN 'fmcg_products.csv' p USING (sku)
WHERE s.on_promotion = 1
GROUP BY p.category
HAVING SUM(s.revenue_ngn) > 1e9
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

AVG(discount_pct) is not the discount you are paying. It is an unweighted average of week-rows, and the money went out at a quite different rate.

When a query is too long to read

If a query cannot be said in English in under twenty seconds, it is doing too much at once to be reviewed reliably.

The fix is to ask for it as a sequence of named steps, each named for what it produces:

“Rewrite this as a sequence of named CTEs, one per logical step, with a comment on each saying what it produces and what its grain is.”

A CTE — common table expression — is simply a temporary named result that the next step builds on. The database does not care either way. The person reviewing it in six months does, and so do you in six months.

2.2 · The laptop warehouse

10:45 — 11:45 · 55,474 rows, no server, no internet

What actually changed

For thirty years, “more data than Excel can hold” meant a project: a server, a licence, a database administrator, and four months.

An analytical database now runs inside your laptop. It reads files where they sit, and in most configurations it needs no administrator rights to install.

It works when the internet does not. In Lagos that is a commercial argument rather than a footnote.

An executive can now verify a number personally — twenty minutes and a copy of the extract. That changes the politics of every number in the building.

What to tell your CIO

It does not replace the warehouse. It replaces the waiting.


The warehouse is where definitions are agreed, history is retained, access is governed and lineage is recorded. A laptop engine does none of that and should not be asked to.

What goes away is the two-week queue for an ad-hoc extract.

Three commands, four seconds, every new file

DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT (week_starting, depot_code, sku)) AS distinct_grain,
       MIN(week_starting), MAX(week_starting)
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

55,474 rows. 55,260 distinct grains. And 789 nulls in units_sold, in a file with 10 genuine zeros.

Neither of those appears in any summary anybody hands you. Both take four seconds to find.

2.3 · Excel as the bridge

11:45 — 12:45 · Demoted from engine, promoted to interface

Excel is not wrong. It is in the wrong place.

Still the best tool in the world for

  • Small, judgement-heavy modelling that a CFO pokes at live
  • The last mile of a number, where formatting and context matter
  • Universal interchange — everyone can open it
  • Twenty numbers, four minutes, one answer

Where it should stop

  • As a database — the authoritative source of a fact
  • As a pipeline — fourteen sheets run by hand, in an order one person remembers
  • At scale — four hundred thousand rows cannot be reviewed by eye
  • Where a single-cell edit silently changes a total

Power Query is a pipeline. A step list is a sequence of named steps, exactly like the CTEs from this morning. People who know Remove Columns → Filter → Group By → Merge already understand the ideas and have never been told so.

The demonstration to watch closely

four minutes, live

Get Data → From Folder → Combine → Filter → Group By → Merge

Note the row count before the merge and after it. Write both down.

Hold that thought until 13:45.

2.4 · Joins that lie

13:45 — 14:45 · The most important session of the week

What a join actually does

A join attaches one table to another by matching a shared key — attaching each sale to the depot it happened in, or each order line to the product it refers to.

A join multiplies. That is what it is for.

Left table Right table What happens
One row per order line One row per product Safe — many-to-one
One row per order line Two rows per product Every line doubles — fan-out
One row per customer Many rows per customer The customer count inflates
One row per day One row per day per region Days multiply by regions

Run this. Do not read ahead.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

SELECT d.region, ROUND(SUM(s.revenue_ngn)/1e9, 2) AS revenue_bn
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
JOIN 'data/fmcg_depots.csv' d USING (depot_code)
GROUP BY d.region ORDER BY revenue_bn DESC;

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
JOIN 'data/fmcg_depots.csv' d USING (depot_code);

Write down the regional ranking before you run the third query. Note which region is second.

What just happened

Rows Abuja Central Region rank
Truth 55,474 ₦4.51bn North Central 4th
After the join 60,094 ₦9.03bn North Central 2nd

Somebody renamed Abuja Central and inserted the new name instead of updating the old row. Every Abuja line matched two dimension rows, and doubled.

Nothing about the query is wrong. Run it past any reviewer, any linter, any assistant, and it passes. The only thing that catches it is counting the rows.

The two questions, for people who never write a join

“One row per what?”

“How many rows before the join, and how many after?”


Ask these in a meeting once, and watch what happens to the quality of what you are shown afterwards.

And the one next door

SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, AVG(on_time) AS on_time_rate,
       SUM(order_value_ngn)/1e9 AS spend_bn
FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY spend_bn DESC;

Nine rows come back. There are eight suppliers.

Consolidated, Cedar is 14.0% of spend and is on time on 98.5% of orders, against a network average of 77.4%. The next best manages 85.9%.

It is the best supplier this business has, and the scorecard shows it as two ordinary halves.

2.5 · Data quality as a contract

14:45 — 15:30 · From “please check the data” to pass or fail

Type checks catch almost nothing that matters

Write business rules that cannot be false if the data is sound.


Receipts follow orders · percentages sum to 100 · a customer cannot churn twice · units are never negative · every transaction has a valid depot · nobody is 126 years old.

received_date < po_date is two perfectly good dates. A duplicated dimension row is a perfectly good row. Almost every defect that costs money is type-valid.

Six rules, three failures

Rule Failures
Fact grain is unique (depot × SKU × week) 214
Depot dimension key is unique 1
Every sale maps to a known depot 0
Units never negative 0
Goods received after they are ordered 126
A discount implies a promotion 0

A suite where everything passes on the first run has probably not been written honestly.

Every rule gets a severity

Fatal — the analysis is invalid. Stop the pipeline. (The grain is not unique.)

Warn — proceed, with a caveat printed on the output. (126 negative lead times, 1.4% of orders, excluded and noted.)

Note — logged and trended, so that a slow drift becomes visible. (The null rate was 1.2% last month and is 1.4% now.)

Without severities, teams either stop the pipeline constantly or turn the checks off altogether. The second one happens quietly, and usually about six weeks in.

Lab 2 · The pipeline that reruns

15:45 — 16:45

Raw files in, one tested table out. Then delete the output and run it again.

  1. Read raw, types stated, nothing guessed
  2. Dedupe to the stated grain — and comment why
  3. Fix the dimension
  4. The contract runs, and stops the pipeline if it fails
  5. Join with a row-count assertion
  6. Write Parquet

Then hand your script to the next table and have them run it on their machine. That is where most pipelines fail on the first Tuesday, and it is worth finding today.

Close

Capstone checkpoint: your pipeline runs.


Even if what comes out of it is trivial. A pipeline producing one correct row on Tuesday is worth more than a beautiful model on Thursday that nobody can reproduce.

Two failure logbook entries today. This day earns them.
